title: Holocaust Remembrance Day
hook: on the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz, the world remembers the Jews murdered in the Holocaust and all the Nazis' victims

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Ashura: a fast for Moses' rescue, and mourning for Husayn. Your line was remembered grief.

Someone steps up to a microphone with a printed list and reads a name. A first name, a family name, a town. Then the next person reads another. Nobody makes a speech. Nobody explains. The names keep coming, one voice after another, and the room just listens. Ceremonies like this happen on days set aside to remember the Holocaust: the murder of Europe's Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators, and the murder of many others alongside them. Today is about why a single name matters so much there.
screen: `A PRINTED LIST.` → `ONE NAME, THEN ANOTHER.` → `NOBODY MAKES A SPEECH.`

segments.voice: First, the day. In a resolution, the United Nations General Assembly set an international day of remembrance on the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz, in January. It remembers the Jews who were murdered, along with members of other minorities. Among the Nazis' other victims were Roma and disabled people. Israel and Jewish communities also keep their own day of remembrance, Yom HaShoah, in the spring. Second, a place and a name. The Holocaust memorial in Jerusalem is called Yad Vashem, words taken from the book of Isaiah. In the King James Bible, God promises people who feared they would leave nothing behind: "Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off." A place, and a name, that shall not be cut off. Third, why names. The scale of the Holocaust is so vast that the mind can go blank before it, the way it can go numb before distant suffering, as this path heard a few days ago. A name undoes that. A name had a kitchen, a street, a favorite song, someone who called it at dinnertime. Reading one name turns a number back into a person. Fourth, remembering as a duty. Some survivors spoke and wrote so that what happened would not be forgotten or denied. Remembering here is not dwelling. It is keeping faith with people who were meant to vanish without a trace, and keeping watch over the present, so that hatred is recognized early.
screen: `A DAY THE WORLD SET ASIDE.` · `A PLACE AND A NAME.` · `A NAME TURNS A NUMBER INTO A PERSON.` · `KEEPING FAITH WITH THE MURDERED.` · then, large: `REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: If you can do it safely, light a candle, or picture one, and sit with the flame for a few breaths. Let it stand in for one person murdered in the Holocaust, someone you haven't met yet; memorials keep online lists of names and stories for exactly this. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.
Yad Vashem, the Holocaust memorial in Jerusalem, its name from Isaiah's promise of a place and a name that shall not be cut off. Today's word.
Your line: remember. Names keep the people, not just the numbers. That's day seven hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: On Holocaust remembrance days, communities, schools and governments hold ceremonies where names of victims are read aloud, candles are lit, and survivors' testimonies are heard; Jewish communities also keep Yom HaShoah in the spring.
